enc.title: Celestial coordinates: where is a star in the sky?

blocks.html: The equatorial system projects Earth’s latitude and longitude onto the sky. Declination $\delta$ is the angle north (+) or south (−) of the celestial equator, $-90^\circ\le\delta\le90^\circ$. Right ascension $\alpha$ is measured eastward along the equator from the vernal equinox, in hours: $24^{\rm h}=360^\circ$, $1^{\rm h}=15^\circ$.

blocks.label: hour angle; pole altitude = latitude; altitude at culmination

blocks.html: A star is circumpolar (never sets) for an observer at northern latitude $\varphi$ if $\delta>90^\circ-\varphi$, and never rises if $\delta<-(90^\circ-\varphi)$.

Galactic coordinates $(l,b)$: latitude $b$ from the Galactic plane, longitude $l$ from the direction of the Galactic centre (in Sagittarius). Extinction and star counts depend mainly on $|b|$: looking along the disk ($b\approx0$) passes through much more dust.

Right ascension is a clock: a star with $\alpha=6^{\rm h}$ crosses your meridian 6 sidereal hours after the vernal equinox does. Declination is fixed for a star, so $h_{\max}$ only depends on where you stand.
1 hour of RA is $15^\circ$ of arc only on the equator; on the sky the arc between two RAs shrinks by $\cos\delta$.
MC style: which stars are visible from Zurich ($\varphi\approx47^\circ$), how high does a star culminate, why extinction grows towards $b=0$.

blocks.html: Looking at the solar disk at angle $ heta$ from the normal ($\mu=\cos heta$), we see down to optical depth $ au\approx\mu$ along the vertical: the Eddington-Barbier relation $I_ u(0,\mu)\approx S_ u( au_ u=\mu)$, exact for a linear source function $S=a+b au$.

At the limb ($\mu\to0$) we only see shallow, cooler layers, so the limb is darker: $I(0)/I(1)=0.4$ in this model, close to the observed solar value in the visible. $T=T_{\rm eff}$ at $\tau=\frac23$: the “photosphere”.
Opacity laws. Electron (Thomson) scattering is grey and independent of $\rho,T$; bound-free and free-free absorption follow Kramers’ law; the H$^-$ ion dominates in the cool solar atmosphere.
Kramers opacity falls steeply with $T$: hot, massive stars and the deep interior are dominated by electron scattering, which is why the Eddington luminosity uses $\kappa_{\rm es}$.
$n_e/\rho=(1+X)/(2m_p)$ for fully ionised H and He: each H gives one electron per $m_p$, each He two electrons per $4m_p$.
MC style: why is the solar limb darker; which opacity sets $L_{\rm Edd}$; units of $\kappa$.

blocks.html: Matter falling from far away onto a compact object of mass $M$ and radius $R$ releases its potential energy. In a thin disk, half is radiated on the way in (virial: the other half is orbital kinetic energy), the rest at the surface (if there is one).

Efficiency: neutron star ($1.4M_\odot$, 10 km) $\eta\approx0.2$, far above hydrogen burning ($0.007$); white dwarf ($R\sim10^4$ km) $\eta\sim10^{-4}$. A black hole has no surface; a thin disk reaches $\eta\approx0.06$-$0.4$ depending on spin.

Each ring radiates nearly as a blackbody at $T(r)$; the sum is a stretched blackbody. For neutron stars and stellar black holes the inner disk reaches $\sim10^7$ K: X-ray binaries. The accretion rate is capped where $L_{\rm acc}=L_{\rm Edd}$.
The deeper the potential well ($M/R$), the more energy per kilogram: compact objects turn infalling gas into the brightest X-ray sources in the Galaxy.
$T\propto r^{-3/4}$ comes from the dissipation rate $\propto GM\dot M/r^3$ per unit area; it is not the virial temperature of the gas.
Typical: accretion luminosity and efficiency of a neutron star, Eddington-limited $\dot M$, black-hole growth time (HS25 winter Q6).

enc.title: Epicycles, the Oort limit and asymmetric drift

blocks.html: A star on a nearly circular orbit oscillates radially around its guiding centre with the epicycle frequency $\kappa$. With $\Omega=v_c/R$ and the Oort constants $A=\frac12\left(\frac{v_c}R-\frac{dv_c}{dR}\right)$, $B=-\frac12\left(\frac{v_c}R+\frac{dv_c}{dR}\right)$:

Oort limit. Vertical Jeans equation plus Poisson for a thin disk: tracer stars with density $n(z)$ and dispersion $\langle v_z^2\rangle$ measure the vertical force, and hence the total local mass density $\rho_0$.

Comparing $\rho_0$ (about $0.1M_\odot\,{\rm pc^{-3}}$) with the stars and gas actually counted shows there is little room for dark matter in the disk; the dark halo is round and its local density small.

Asymmetric drift. Populations with larger velocity dispersion are partly supported by “pressure” and rotate more slowly than the local circular speed. The radial Jeans equation gives $v_c^2-\bar v_\varphi^2\approx2v_cv_a\propto\sigma_R^2$: the lag $v_a$ grows with $\sigma_R^2$ (Strömberg).

Old, hot populations (halo stars) lag far behind the Sun; young, cold ones (gas, OB stars) co-rotate. The Sun’s motion relative to the local standard of rest is found by extrapolating to $\sigma\to0$.
The Oort limit measures the total density (stars + gas + dark matter) near the Sun, not the visible part.
Recent exams test the Jeans equations through the Plummer sphere (HS25 winter Q4); know which equation gives what.

blocks.html: A source moving with speed $\beta c$ at angle $\theta$ to our line of sight emits most of its radiation into a cone of half-angle $\sim1/\gamma$ around its velocity.

Observed flux is boosted by a high power of $\mathcal D$ (about $\mathcal D^{3+\alpha}$ for a moving blob with spectrum $F_\nu\propto\nu^{-\alpha}$): a jet pointing at us (blazar) outshines its counter-jet by orders of magnitude.

With $\gamma\beta>1$, knots in quasar jets appear to move faster than light across the sky. Nothing moves faster than $c$: the source nearly catches up with its own light, so the arrival times are compressed.
Beaming explains why one-sided jets are common and why the same AGN looks like a blazar, a quasar or a radio galaxy depending on viewing angle (unification).
$\beta_{\rm app}$ is maximal at $\cos\theta=\beta$, not at $\theta=0$: head-on motion has no transverse component.
MC style: why superluminal motion does not violate relativity; synchrotron as the emission mechanism of jets (HS24 summer, HS25 winter).

enc.title: What dark matter can be, and the intergalactic medium

blocks.html: Dark matter is classified by its speed when structures start to grow. Hot dark matter (light neutrinos) is relativistic at decoupling and free-streams out of small perturbations: only very large structures form first (top-down). Cold dark matter (e.g. WIMPs) is slow: small halos form first and merge (bottom-up, hierarchical), which matches observations.

Neutrinos with $\sum m_\nu\lesssim1$ eV give $\Omega_\nu\ll\Omega_m$: real, but not the dominant dark matter. Baryons are limited by BBN to $\Omega_bh^2\approx0.022$, far below $\Omega_mh^2\approx0.14$: most dark matter is non-baryonic.

Intergalactic medium. Hydrogen clouds between us and a quasar absorb Ly$\alpha$ ($121.6$ nm in the rest frame) at their own redshift, observed at $121.6(1+z_{\rm abs})$ nm: a Lyman-$\alpha$ forest blueward of the quasar’s emission line.

Gunn-Peterson test. Even a tiny fraction of neutral H spread smoothly would absorb everything blueward of Ly$\alpha$. No such trough is seen below $z\approx6$, so the IGM is highly ionised; the trough appears at $z\gtrsim6$, the end of reionisation.
A quasar is a flashlight shining through the whole history of the IGM; each absorption line is a cloud at a different distance.
The forest lies at wavelengths shorter than the quasar’s own Ly$\alpha$ line: absorbers are closer, so less redshifted.
MC style: hot vs cold dark matter, evidence for non-baryonic dark matter, what the Ly$\alpha$ forest is.

enc.title: Binary evolution and the Algol paradox

blocks.html: In a close binary each star sits in its Roche lobe, the region where its own gravity dominates in the rotating frame. The lobes touch at the inner Lagrange point $L_1$.

When a star expands after the main sequence and fills its Roche lobe, gas flows through $L_1$ onto the companion, directly or via an accretion disk. Mass transfer can reverse which star is the heavier one.

Algol paradox. In Algol the less massive star is the more evolved (a subgiant), against single-star evolution. Resolution: it was originally the more massive, evolved first, and has transferred most of its mass to the companion.

blocks.label: why the heavier star evolves first

blocks.html: End states: a white dwarf accreting from a companion can give novae (surface hydrogen ignition) or, near the Chandrasekhar mass, a type Ia supernova; neutron stars and black holes accreting from companions are X-ray binaries.
A binary is a stellar-evolution experiment with mass transfer as an extra knob: ages from single-star tracks fail for interacting pairs.
Type Ia supernovae come from white dwarfs in binaries (no hydrogen lines), not from the core collapse of massive stars.
MC style: Algol paradox, which binaries give SN Ia or X-ray sources.
